item.title: Pairwise Compatibility Graphs of Unweighted Caterpillars
item.description: arXiv:2610.14681v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper we study pairwise compatibility graphs whose witness tree is required to be an unweighted caterpillar. This is a natural restriction of PCGs, in the same line of research as the study of star witnesses, which led to the class of double-threshold graphs. In the caterpillar case, we show that this restriction is equivalent to a one-dimensional difference-labelling problem: a graph admits such a representation if and only if its vertices can be assigned integer labels so that adjacency is determined exactly by whether the absolute difference of two labels belongs to a given interval. Using this characterization, we derive structural properties of the class, including bounded twin-width, and study its relation with familiar graph families. We show that the class contains cycles and two-dimensional grids, while it excludes natural obstructions such as the subdivided star $S_{2,2,2,2,2}$, the cube graph $Q_3$, the wheel $W_6$, and the complement of the $3$-sunlet. We also consider restricted representations, including centipede witnesses and representations with a given interval and we give a polynomial-time recognition algorithm when the interval is fixed.
item.dc:creator: Cyriac Antony, Manuel Lafond, Angelo Monti, Blerina Sinaimeri

item.title: Almost every Boolean function has central threshold degree
item.description: arXiv:2610.15057v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The polynomial threshold degree (or threshold degree) of a Boolean function is the least degree of a real polynomial whose sign represents it. We prove that almost every Boolean function has polynomial threshold degree among the central one or two integers. More precisely, a uniformly chosen Boolean function on $n$ variables has threshold degree $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ or $\lceil n/2\rceil$ except with probability at most $\exp(-c2^{n/2}/n)$, for an absolute constant $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$. A parity example gives a lower bound on the exceptional probability whose exponent differs from ours by a factor of order $n$. The proof relates polynomial sign representation to recovery of Reed--Muller codes from random erasures, and combines sharp-threshold estimates with bounds on generalized Hamming weights and minimum distance.
item.dc:creator: Martin Anthony

item.title: A Four-by-Four Obstruction to Polynomial Removal for Ordered Binary Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2610.15370v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We exhibit a fixed $4\times 4$ binary matrix with no polynomial induced ordered removal bound. At depth $h\geq 1$, let $m=2^h$. Our explicit host has order $(14h+2)m$, exactly $2m^6+\frac{1}{2}(m-2)m^5$ induced copies, and exact editing distance $m^2$ cells. Its normalized editing distance is $\Theta(h^{-2})$, while its induced-copy density is $\Theta(4^{-h}h^{-8})$. The lower bound holds against arbitrary cell edits through an injective family of $m^2$ protected selections. An exhaustive arithmetic classification identifies every induced copy and proves that a matching canonical repair creates none. The original-copy transversal number is exactly $m$, yielding an unbounded gap between hitting existing copies and eliminating all copies. The identities and the obstruction at every depth are formalized in Lean, with verification sources included as ancillary files.
item.dc:creator: Zinan Wang

item.title: Period Piece: NEXPTIME-complete problems on digraphs via Boolean network dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.16561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The central object in this work is the Boolean network, a function $f:\{0,1\}^V \to \{0,1\}^V$. Often identified with $f$ is its dynamics $D_f$, the digraph with exactly $\{x \to y : f(x)=y\}$ as its arcs. The interaction graph of $f$ is the digraph $G$ on $V$ which can be thought of as representing the dependencies of the components of $f$ on one another. On the other hand, model-checking is a major field of study in graph algorithms and complexity. We consider problems at the intersection of these paradigms: for a given property $\phi$, we say that a digraph $G$ is $\phi$-dynamic if $G$ is the interaction graph of some Boolean network $f$ such that $D_f \models \phi$. The corresponding decision problem $\phi$-DYNAMIC asks whether $G$ is $\phi$-dynamic. Problems of this form are well-studied in the Boolean networks community. For example, it is a well-known result that, letting $\phi$ be 'No fixed points' (i.e. $\nexists x:x\to x$), $\phi$-DYNAMIC is equivalent to the structural digraph problem NON-ACYCLIC, which is solvable in linear time. We establish, for the first time, properties $\phi$ for which $\phi$-DYNAMIC is computationally hard. These include the 'Unique fixed point' property $\exists!x:x\to x$, and a range of properties concerning the periodic points of $f$ (i.e. vertices of $D_f$ which lie on a cycle). More widely, we exhibit an infinite family of natural properties $\phi$ such that $\phi$-DYNAMIC is $\mathrm{NEXPTIME}$-complete, which we call PERIOD PIECE. As a special case, these include all properties of the form 'Unique cycle of length $k$' and 'Exactly $k$ fixed points' for any $k \ge 1$. On the other hand, we show that if the input digraph has bounded in-degree, then for those same problems $\phi$-DYNAMIC collapses down to $\mathrm{NP}^{\mathrm{NP}}$, the second level of the polynomial hierarchy, though it remains $\mathrm{NP}^{\mathrm{NP}}$-complete.
item.dc:creator: Florian Bridoux, Maximilien Gadouleau, David C. Kutner, Adrien Richard

item.title: A note on Finiteness and Boundedness in Cartesian Products of Discrete and Well-Ordered Sets, Application to Transition Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.16764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this short note, we prove that any closed interval in a well-ordered and discrete space is finite. The coincidence between finiteness and boundedness can then be established for transition systems where the state space is well-ordered and discrete. Finally, this result is also proven when the state space is a Cartesian product of $d$ discrete and well-ordered sets.
item.dc:creator: Gerard Memmi

item.title: Graph Distortion Distances, Gromov-Hausdorff and the Hardness of Gromov-Wasserstein
item.description: arXiv:2610.16926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the computational complexity of graph distortion distances, a family of graph metrics measuring how vertex distances differ between two graphs. Formally, these distances are defined in terms of standard matrix norms on the difference of distance matrices under an optimal vertex alignment. The resulting metrics have natural interpretations, corresponding to three ways of measuring the distortion of shortest-path distances: the maximum distortion among all vertex pairs (entrywise maximum norm), global aggregation (entrywise $p$-norms), and local aggregation (operator $p$-norms) of distortions. For maximum distortion, we show that approximation below a factor of two is NP-hard even for highly restricted trees. Due to the close connection to the Gromov-Hausdorff distance, we obtain a similar hardness result for the latter. In both cases, we show essentially optimal additive inapproximability. On the algorithmic side, we give a subcubic-time algorithm for optimal embeddings of connected graphs into paths, based on a structural decomposition along a diametral path. Additionally, we give a simple approximation algorithm when one input graph has a "relatively path-like" metric structure, i.e. has bounded pathlength. For local and global distortion, we derive various hardness results even for restricted inputs. Making use of a close connection between the global distortion distances and Gromov-Wasserstein distances, we give the first formal proof of NP-hardness of the latter, which has been claimed in the literature many times but has, to the best of our knowledge, never been correctly proven.
item.dc:creator: Jens Breitung, Timo Gervens, Julius P\"orzgen

item.title: On Collusion-Free Teaching in Planar Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.18714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-clashing teaching minimizes teaching complexity among models satisfying the Goldman--Mathias collusion-avoidance criterion. While the Vapnik--Chervonenkis dimension (VCdim) measures the complexity of learning from samples, non-clashing teaching dimension (NCTD) measures the number of examples required when a teacher can select them. Whether NCTD is always bounded above by VCdim remains a fundamental open question in learning theory. In this paper, we investigate this question for the concept classes of closed neighborhoods in planar graphs. We prove a tight upper bound of two on their NCTD, thereby establishing the conjectured inequality for this family. For the positive variant NCTD+, in which teaching sets contain only positive examples, we obtain a tight upper bound of four. Finally, we show that deciding whether either NCTD+ or NCTD is at most one is NP-complete, even for concept classes of closed neighborhoods in planar graphs. In particular, despite the upper bound of two on NCTD for such classes, distinguishing between NCTD values of one and two remains NP-hard.
item.dc:creator: Khazaliya Liana, Kuske Clemens

item.title: Satisfiability and freezing in random integer programs
item.description: arXiv:2610.14085v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a model of a random centrally symmetric polytope and ask about the existence of points in the polytope with non-zero, integer coordinates. Our main results are the location of a sharp threshold for the existence of these integer points, a characterization of the typical empirical distribution of their coordinates, and showing that near the feasibility threshold these integer points are almost always totally isolated --- at linear Hamming distance to the nearest other integer point in the polytope. The behavior of these random integer programs is related to that of the symmetric binary perceptron (the case when coordinates of points are $\pm 1$-valued). The lack of symmetry in the set of potential solutions leads to new questions and phenomena, such as the distribution of the coordinate sizes in typical solutions, and requires the development of new information-theoretic techniques to deal with higher-dimensional optimization problems arising in the method of moments.
item.dc:creator: Dylan J. Altschuler, Ruben Ascoli, Will Perkins

item.title: Maximally symmetric $(23_4)$ configurations and the end of the existence problem for geometric $(n_4)$ configurations
item.description: arXiv:2610.14099v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A geometric $(n_4)$ configuration is a set of $n$ points and $n$ lines in the real projective plane such that every point lies on exactly four of the lines and every line contains exactly four of the points. The question of which $n$ admit such a configuration was posed by Gr\"unbaum in 2000, following his 1990 paper with Rigby that gave the first geometric $4$-configuration, a $(21_4)$. Successive work of Bokowski-Schewe, of Bokowski, Gr\"unbaum and Schewe, of Bokowski-Pilaud, and of Cuntz settled every case but one. Cuntz's 2018 paper, which constructed $(22_4)$ and $(26_4)$ configurations, states that only $n=23$ remained open. We settle this last case. We prove that for every prime $n\equiv3\pmod4$, in particular for $n=23$, the group of projective symmetries of a geometric $(n_4)$ configuration has order at most four, which explains why $n=23$ resisted the symmetric constructions that settled the other values. Reducing the case of a Klein four-group of symmetries to a few thousand bilinear polynomial systems in $18$ unknowns, and solving all of them exactly with Gr\"obner bases and saturation, we show that exactly two geometric $(23_4)$ configurations reach this bound, up to projective equivalence, and that there are no others even over $\mathbb{C}$. Both are self-polar with respect to a conic. The first has integer homogeneous coordinates; the second is defined over $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{17})$, but not over $\mathbb{Q}$. Consequently geometric $(n_4)$ configurations exist if and only if $n\ge18$ and $n\ne19$. A third configuration, self-polar and defined over a real cubic field, has only a single symmetry of order two. The same classification at $n=22$ and $n=26$ recovers Cuntz's configurations and finds three new combinatorial types at $n=22$ and $94$ at $n=26$, among them a $(26_4)$ configuration that is self-polar with respect to a conic without real points.
item.dc:creator: Wenhao Lu

item.title: The Path Partition Conjecture and 3-(quasi-)Transitive Digraphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.14217v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A digraph $D = (V,E)$ is 3-transitive (respectively, 3-quasi-transitive) if whenever $(u,v,w,z)$ is a directed path of length 3, $(u,z) \in E$ (respectively, $(u,z) \in E$ or $(z,u) \in E$). These digraphs extend the concepts of transitive and quasi-transitive digraphs, respectively. For 3-transitive and 3-quasi-transitive digraphs, only the strong case has been characterized. In this paper, we introduce the notion of semi-acyclic digraphs and use it to describe completely the structure of 3-transitive and 3-quasi-transitive digraphs. As an application of this type of structure description, we prove that the path partition conjecture holds for the class of extended semi-acyclic digraphs, which generalizes two previously known results on the conjecture.
item.dc:creator: Shamik Ghosh, Jing Huang

item.title: Coefficientwise Extremality and Rigidity for Independent Sets in Bipartite Graph Covers
item.description: arXiv:2610.14892v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Let $G$ be a finite bipartite graph and let $\widetilde G$ be an $M$-fold cover. We compare independent sets of $\widetilde G$ with those of the trivial cover, consisting of $M$ disjoint copies of $G$, after prescribing how many vertices are selected above each vertex of $G$. A conjecture from 2011, motivated by the Bethe approximation, asserts that the trivial cover maximizes every such count. We prove this for every feasible occupation profile whose active graph has treewidth at most two or is chordal bipartite. Equality holds exactly when the restricted cover is flat, meaning that fibre relabelings make it trivial. For $M\ge2$ and positive feasible occupations, a nonflat cover of a connected bipartite graph of treewidth at most two has a deficit of at least twice the coefficient of $p_G^{M-2}$ with every occupation reduced by one. A holonomy-dependent bound improves the factor to three for odd-order holonomy; both uniform constants are sharp. Comparison and rigidity survive finite compositions along an edge or a vertex, and quantitative bounds from one piece propagate to the whole graph, giving results beyond the two original classes. On any bipartite base, the first nonzero homogeneous defect is determined by the shortest cycles with nontrivial holonomy. At singleton occupations, our counts are numbers of DP-colorings of full covers. The dual DP color function on these classes and their finite seam compositions equals the chromatic polynomial, with equality attained precisely by canonical labelings. Dong's chromatic-polynomial inequality then yields the Dual-DP Shameful inequality on the same graph class. The main theorems have been formalized in Lean 4.
item.dc:creator: Yusuke Watanabe

item.title: Non-convex integer programming: a deterministic solution method of the large block sale problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.14962v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a non-convex, nonlinear integer mathematical program with a linear constraint. This problem originates in finance and consists of selling a large predetermined quantity of a financial asset over a fixed time horizon, while maximizing the total proceeds. The selling price is modeled using a deterministic penalty function capturing the market's adverse reaction to the selling flow. From a complexity perspective, the problem is in NP. We first solve the problem exactly using dynamic programming and propose several heuristics that yield tight numerical lower bounds. We then reformulate the problem into an equivalent factorable form and derive a tight convex relaxation using McCormick inequalities. This relaxation is embedded within an adapted Branch & Bound algorithm to find the global optimum in finite time. Numerical experiments show that our methods outperform several widely used generic solvers (LocalSolver, Scip, Baron, Couenne, and Bonmin) for selected instances, but do not yield tight upper bounds, beyond small instances.
item.dc:creator: David Nizard, Dominique Quadri

item.title: Sharp bounds and extremal structure of minimally strongly $k$-connected digraphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.14979v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Let $D$ be a finite simple minimally strongly $k$-connected digraph, where $k\ge 2$, and let $n=|V(D)|$. Mader proved in 1985 that $|A(D)|\le 2k(n-k)$ for all sufficiently large $n$, with equality if and only if $D\cong \overleftrightarrow{K}_{k,n-k}$ (JCTB 1985). We prove that this bound holds whenever $n\ge 3k-1$ and that the order threshold $3k-1$ is best possible. Moreover, if $n\ge 3k$, then equality holds if and only if $D\cong \overleftrightarrow{K}_{k,n-k}$. The threshold $3k$ is also best possible. These results resolve the conjecture of Mader in (JCTB 1985).
item.dc:creator: Junran Yu, Gregory Gutin, Hong-Jian Lai, Xiaoyan Zhang

item.title: Nim heaps in the Game of Cycles: the parity conjecture fails on trees
item.description: arXiv:2610.15145v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Game of Cycles, invented by Francis Su, is a two-player game in which the players take turns drawing arrows on the edges of a plane graph, never creating a sink or a source. On a tree only the sink-source rule matters, and the player who makes the last move wins. Several authors conjectured that on a tree the second player wins exactly when the number of markable edges is even. We show that this parity conjecture is false, and we explain why. The explanation is a hidden game of Nim: a path segment that is blocked by an arrow at one end and free at the other behaves exactly like a nim heap whose size is its length. Combined with a calculus for cutting and gluing trees at vertices next to leaves, this shows that the conjecture fails as soon as a single tree has Grundy value at least 2. The smallest counterexamples have 15 vertices. Trees with Grundy values 2 and 4 first appear at 17 vertices, and every value up to 63 occurs, which answers a question of Fokkink and Zandee. We also refute a related conjecture of Zandee. We then look closely at spiders. The spiders S(2,3,z) violate the conjecture for every z >= 14. The Grundy values of S(1,2j,z) are given by an exact formula governed by binary carries. For 99 pairs (x,y), the value of S(x,y,z) is eventually the parity of z. On the positive side, the conjecture holds for all trees in which every thread has at most two edges, and this bound is sharp. Along the way we prove a twin-branch reduction, give an algorithm that is polynomial for spiders with a fixed number of legs, and collect the questions that we could not answer. The boldest asks whether every non-negative integer is the Grundy value of some tree.
item.dc:creator: Muchen Xu

item.title: A Fast Greedy Algorithm with a 0.45 Approximation Guarantee for the Airplane Refueling Problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.15222v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a natural greedy algorithm for the Airplane Refueling Problem (ARP), based on a well-known priority rule. We show that this algorithm achieves an approximation guarantee of $9/20$, noticeably improving the previously known $1/12$ guarantee for a fast algorithm. We also show that the same priority rule can be implemented in $O(n\log n)$ time and $O(n)$ space using a dynamic convex-hull data structure. These results provide a worst-case approximation guarantee for an existing greedy priority rule and establish an efficient implementation. In the real-RAM model, the running-time bound is independent of the magnitude of the processing times. The resulting method is also suitable as a fast primal routine inside more complex exact and approximation algorithms for large instances. These results narrow the gap between theoretically strong but complex approximation schemes and lightweight algorithms that can be used directly in computational pipelines. The algorithm combines a simple selection rule with a provable performance bound, making it a useful baseline for further algorithmic studies of ARP.
item.dc:creator: Oleg Lomachenko, Arnold Enikeev

item.title: FirstFit coloring process of random bipartite graphs and an online coloring lower bound in the random order model
item.description: arXiv:2610.15468v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: FirstFit colors each arriving vertex with the smallest positive integer absent from its previously colored neighborhood. We prove that this rule can require $n^{\Omega(1)}$ many colors on certain bipartite graph of $n$ vertices even when the vertices arrive in a uniformly random order. This refutes the conjecture of Bosek, Gutowski, Laso\'{n}, and Przyby\l{}o [BGLP24] that FirstFit uses a polylogarithmic expected number of colors on every bipartite graph in the random order model. We obtain the lower bound by analyzing the FirstFit coloring process on random bipartite graphs, where vertices arrive to either side with equal probability, and with an independent edge density $n^{-x}$ for some $0 < x < 1$. Our result can also be viewed as a qualitative strengthening of Ku\v{c}era [Ku\v{c}91], who showed that, for every $\epsilon > 0$, there are graphs with chromatic number at most $n^{\epsilon}$ on which FirstFit uses $\Omega(n/\log n)$ colors in expectation under a uniformly random order. Our result shows that such poor behavior of FirstFit already occurs for $\chi(G) = 2$.
item.dc:creator: Yaqiao Li, Xin Li

item.title: A Quantum Analogue of the Covering Lemma: Limits of Exact Anonymous Computation
item.description: arXiv:2610.15601v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can quantum communication determine the size of an anonymous network when no size bound is known? Classical impossibility proofs rely on the covering lemma: an execution can be reproduced on a larger network with the same local structure. Quantum interference invalidates this argument - a measurement record possible on a network can become impossible on a cover. We show that the impossibility of exact counting nevertheless survives. Our main result is a quantum analogue of the covering lemma that preserves local possibilities rather than complete executions. Within a cyclic covering family, every local measurement outcome possible at a node remains possible at a corresponding node in every sufficiently large network. This holds even after information has travelled around the smaller network, beyond the reach of a simple locality argument. We extend the principle to the universal covering tree and finite covers with sufficiently long cycles. The proof combines tensor-network methods with graph coverings: a common representation across network sizes turns normalization into a constraint on which local outcomes can occur. For uniform synchronous protocols with independently prepared nodes, this support-lifting principle rules out zero-error counting and even the production of a guaranteed finite size bound on anonymous rings and the other cyclic covering families considered here. It also rules out exact leader election with termination in finite time with probability one on these families. Measurements, classical control, and local memory growing with time are allowed; no predetermined running-time bound is assumed. Quantum interference thus defeats execution lifting without enabling infallible certification of network size.
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe Di Molfetta, Petra Camilli

item.title: Binary Codes Correcting Multiple Edits via Polynomial Hashing and Entropy Recycling
item.description: arXiv:2610.15631v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Codes in the Levenshtein metric that can correct multiple edits (including deletions, insertions, and substitutions) have attracted a lot of attention recently owing to their application in DNA-based storage and racetrack memories. In this work, we present new techniques for designing explicit binary codes of length $n$ that correct $t$ edits with at most $(2t+1)\log n+O_t(\log\log n)$ bits of redundancy. We first propose to use a polynomial hash to construct a systematic code that corrects $t$ edits with $(4t+2)\log n+O_t(\log\log n)$ bits of redundancy. Then we observe that there are many polynomial hashes like this, some are good, some are bad. So, we propose the second technique, called entropy recycling, to use the indices of good hashes to carry information. As a consequence, we obtain a partial-systematic code of length $n$ that corrects $t$ edits with at most $(2t+1)\log n+O_t(\log\log n)$ bits of redundancy. Finally, we provide deterministic polynomial-time encoding and decoding algorithms for our code.
item.dc:creator: Quan D. Bui, Shuche Wang, Van Khu Vu

item.title: Dynamic Conflict Clustering with Lightweight Learning and Strategic Repair for Distributed Constraint Satisfaction
item.description: arXiv:2610.15658v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Distributed Constraint Satisfaction Problems (DCSPs) model distributed decision-making in multi-agent systems, where agents assign values to local variables while satisfying shared constraints. However, many DCSP solvers still rely on broad, repeated peer-to-peer communication and are largely reactive, with limited support for strategic coordination or learning. This increases communication overhead, can lead to stagnation, and reduces the success of hard instances. Hence, we propose Dynamic Conflict Clustering-Incomplete (DCC-Incomplete), a repair-based solver that combines conflict-centred decomposition, structured coordination, strategic repair, and lightweight learning for stagnation recovery. DCC-Incomplete groups the unsolved part of the problem into conflict clusters and restricts communication via a coordination layer to agents within the same conflict region. It also introduces memory-guided restart, enabling agents and clusters to pause, revise, and adapt repairs based on neighbouring conflict states. A thorough evaluation of DCC-Incomplete on distributed graph-colouring benchmarks with planted satisfying assignments shows that its memory-guided restart improves the success rate from 37.50% to 61.11%, reduces median runtime from 0.565s to 0.367s, and cuts median communication from 12.493 to 6.503 messages per constraint. These results suggest that dynamic conflict clustering, combined with lightweight strategic and learning-guided repair, improves both communication efficiency and robustness in incomplete DCSP solving.
item.dc:creator: Raziyeh Moghaddas, Fabio Caraffini

item.title: Two Linear Programs are Better than One
item.description: arXiv:2610.15909v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The extension complexity $\operatorname{xc}(P)$ of a polytope $P$ is the minimum number of facets of a polytope that projects onto it. Motivated by the complexity of neural networks, Hertrich and Loho introduced the virtual extension complexity $\operatorname{vxc}(P)$ of a polytope $P$, which is the minimum of $\operatorname{xc}(Q) + \operatorname{xc}(R)$ among all polytopes $Q$ and $R$ such that $P+Q=R$. We show the following results pertaining to virtual extension complexity. First, we resolve the core open problem on the topic by showing the virtual extension complexity can be exponentially smaller than extension complexity. Second, we show there are matroid base polytopes with exponential virtual extension complexity by adapting a semi-algebraic counting argument by Hrube\v{s} that extends the counting arguments of Rothvoss. Finally, we show that the maximum virtual extension complexity of a polygon with $n$ vertices is $\Theta(\sqrt{n})$. This resolves an analogue of a question on extension complexity of Fiorini, Rothvoss, and Tiwary in 2011 in the case of virtual extension complexity.
item.dc:creator: Alexander E. Black, Christoph Hertrich, Stefan Kober, Georg Loho

item.title: QPTAS for Max Weight Independent Set in Graphs with Strongly Edge-Sublinear Separators
item.description: arXiv:2610.16025v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A hereditary graph class has strongly edge-sublinear separators if, for some constant $0 \leqslant b < 1$, every graph in the class with $m$ edges admits a balanced separator of size $\mathcal O(m^b)$. We show that Max Weight Independent Set (MWIS) admits a deterministic quasipolynomial-time approximation scheme (QPTAS) on every such class. In particular, this applies to graphs excluding any fixed graph as an induced minor, by a separator theorem of Korhonen and Lokshtanov [SODA 2024]. Our theorem generalizes the QPTASes for axis-parallel rectangles [Adamaszek and Wiese, FOCS 2013] and polygons [Adamaszek, Har-Peled, and Wiese, JACM 2019], or equivalently for packing connected subgraphs of a planar graph [Pilipczuk, van Leeuwen, and Wiese, Algorithmica 2020]. It also generalizes the QPTAS for MWIS on hereditary classes with strongly sublinear separators measured in vertices [Dvo\v{r}\'ak, EJC 2018; Dvo\v{r}\'ak and Lahiri, ESA 2021], as well as the QPTASes for graphs excluding particular induced minors [Chudnovsky et al., arXiv 2025; Bonnet et al., SWAT 2026; Czy\.zewska et al., arXiv 2026].
item.dc:creator: \'Edouard Bonnet, Yeonsu Chang

item.title: Elementary graphs are chromatic-choosable
item.description: arXiv:2610.16258v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A graph is \emph{elementary} if its edges can be coloured with two colours so that the two edges of every induced path on three vertices receive different colours. Elementary graphs are one of the two basic classes in the Chv\'atal--Sbihi decomposition of claw-free perfect graphs; they include all line graphs of bipartite multigraphs and all complements of bipartite graphs. We prove that every elementary graph $G$ satisfies $\ch(G)=\chi(G)=\omega(G)$, confirming for this class the conjecture of Gravier and Maffray that claw-free graphs are chromatic-choosable. The proof combines the Maffray--Reed description of elementary graphs as augmentations of line graphs of bipartite multigraphs, Galvin's theorem, an extremal (edge-maximal) choice of counterexample, and a Hall-type lemma describing how list colourings of a complete graph minus a matching can fail.
item.dc:creator: Narayanan N, Nandana K. Vasudevan, K. Somasundaram

item.title: Towards a Sum-of-Squares Proof for the Nonexistence of Conway's 99-graph
item.description: arXiv:2610.16266v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conway's $99$-graph is a strongly regular graph with parameters $(v,k,\lambda,\mu) = (99,14,1,2)$ and whose existence has long been an open problem. We use both a sum-of-squares program and the fact that a strongly regular graph with $\lambda = 1, \mu = 2$ has no diamond or $K_{2,3}$ subgraph to derive a loose upper bound for the number of triangles that such a graph could contain. This bound is less than the number of triangles that the graph's spectrum asserts, implying that it does not exist.
item.dc:creator: Joseph Natal, Oleksiy Al-saadi

item.title: Exponential Local Search in Bounded-Occurrence MAX-CSP
item.description: arXiv:2610.16898v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the number of improving steps that local search may require for $(2,2,r)$-MCA (Maximum Constraint Assignment), a bounded-occurrence version of MAX-CSP with valued constraints in which every constraint involves at most two variables, every variable occurs in at most two constraints, and every variable takes one of $r$ values. We consider the flip neighborhood, where two assignments are neighbors if they differ in the value of exactly one variable; moving to such a neighbor is called a flip. Local search repeatedly performs improving flips, that is, flips that strictly increase the objective value, until a local optimum is reached. Our main result is that $(2,2,5)$-MCA has the all-exp property: there is an infinite family of instances with initial assignments for which every sequence of improving flips ending in a local optimum has length exponential in the number of variables. Thus, on these instances, local search requires exponentially many steps regardless of which improving flip is chosen at each step. This is the first all-exp result for $(2,2,r)$-MCA for any value of $r$, and our result extends to every $r\ge 5$. In contrast, for $(2,2,2)$-MCA every sequence of improving flips has length at most quadratic in the number of variables~\cite{Kaz2020,KCJ2020}. We give a short, direct proof of this result.
item.dc:creator: Sophia Heimann, Hung P. Hoang, Stefan Hougardy

item.title: Sensitivity of Rotation Symmetric Boolean Functions via Binary Necklaces
item.description: arXiv:2610.17006v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rotation symmetric Boolean functions are Boolean functions invariant under cyclic permutation of their variables and can be represented by binary necklaces. We express local sensitivity as a weighted bichromatic degree in the necklace quotient and derive an exact formula for the multiplicities between neighboring necklaces. For an odd prime number of variables, we obtain explicit sensitivity formulas and show that multiplicity corrections occur only on an asymptotically negligible family of necklaces. For monomial rotation symmetric Boolean functions, we prove that every odd-degree function has maximum sensitivity, determine the sensitivity of every quadratic function, and determine the sensitivity of the consecutive quartic family. We also determine exactly the sensitivity of cyclic run-threshold functions for arbitrary length and threshold.
item.dc:creator: Yuan Li, Jing Zhang

item.title: Block Sensitivity and Certificate Complexity of Rotation Symmetric Boolean Functions
item.description: arXiv:2610.17100v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study block sensitivity and certificate complexity of rotation symmetric Boolean functions, with particular emphasis on monomial rotation symmetric Boolean functions. We first show that every odd-degree monomial rotation symmetric Boolean function on $n$ variables satisfies $s=bs=C=n$. We then determine sensitivity, block sensitivity, and certificate complexity for every quadratic monomial rotation symmetric Boolean function. For the quadratic function $Q_{n,k}$ generated by $x_0x_k$, we prove, outside the short-orbit case, that \[ C(Q_{n,k})= \begin{cases} n,&4\mid n/\gcd(n,k),\\ n-\gcd(n,k),&4\nmid n/\gcd(n,k). \end{cases} \] Moreover, \(bs(Q_{n,k})=C(Q_{n,k})\) for every quadratic MRS function, and outside the short-orbit case, strict separation \(s<bs=C\) occurs exactly when \[ \frac{n}{\gcd(n,k)}\equiv2\pmod4. \] Finally, for the consecutive quartic family \[ R_n(x)=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z_n}x_ix_{i+1}x_{i+2}x_{i+3}, \] we determine all three measures in every residue class modulo $6$, using the sensitivity formulas and, in one residue class, finite-state results established in our companion preprint~\cite{LiZhangRSBFSensitivity}. In particular, for $r=2,3$ and $6q+r\ge5$ we obtain strict separation, \[ \boxed{s(R_{6q+r})=6q<bs(R_{6q+r})=C(R_{6q+r})=6q+1,\qquad r=2,3.} \] Thus this family gives an infinite collection of rotation symmetric Boolean functions for which sensitivity is strictly smaller than block sensitivity, while block sensitivity and certificate complexity coincide.
item.dc:creator: Yuan Li, Jing Zhang

item.title: Dynamic Run-Out Pricing for Perishable Goods
item.description: arXiv:2610.17416v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: I study a dynamic pricing problem in which a seller with limited inventory must sequentially price a perishable product for arriving customers with heterogeneous valuations. The key difficulty lies in balancing immediate sales against future opportunities under capacity constraints and stochastic customer valuations. I propose a simple, interpretable, and asymptotically optimal dynamic pricing algorithm, called Dynamic Run-Out Pricing (DROP), that adjusts prices in real time based on current inventory and anticipated future demand. Under the assumption that customers' valuations follow bounded or exponential distributions, our theoretical results show that DROP's expected revenue converges to the optimal revenue as market size grows. Unlike traditional notions of near-optimality, where the ratio of the algorithm's revenue to the optimal revenue converges to 1, I show that the absolute difference between the two revenues converges to 0 as the market size increases, underscoring the algorithm's effectiveness. Furthermore, I extend our analysis to heavy-tailed valuation distributions, specifically the Pareto distribution, where standard run-out heuristics severely underprice inventory by ignoring the value of waiting for extreme valuations. To correct this, I introduce the Tail-Aware DROP (TA-DROP) heuristic, which intentionally inflates prices to protect inventory, and I prove that it restores asymptotic optimality with a strict polynomial convergence rate.
item.dc:creator: Farbod Ekbatani

item.title: A Practical Combinatorial Interior Point Method for Minimum-Cost Flow
item.description: arXiv:2610.18328v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In a recent breakthrough, Chen, Kyng, Liu, Peng, Probst Gutenberg, and Sachdeva (arXiv:2203.00671) designed the first almost-linear-time algorithm for minimum-cost flow. Their approach uses an Interior Point Method (IPM) to achieve complexity $m^{1+o(1)}\log U \log C$. However, the $m^{1+o(1)}$ factor hides intricate recursive data structures, large constants and multiple log factors. In this paper, we give an implementation following the core ideas of their IPM with practical data structures and empirically obtained decision rules. We compare our solver with the cost scaling and network simplex solvers of LEMON on the instance families of the DIMACS Flow Challenge 2.0 core benchmark. Our implementation scales competitively on five of twelve families and better on two. On grid_wide we observe close to linear scaling: $m^{1.04}$ against $m^{1.48}$ for LEMON. We read these results as first evidence that the almost-linear-time framework can be relevant in practice, discuss our insights gained during the implementation process, and motivate where future work should focus to bridge the theory-practice gap.
item.dc:creator: Emil Sch\"atzle, Simon Meierhans, Rasmus Kyng, Maximilian Probst Gutenberg

item.title: PSPACE-completeness of the Hunters and Rabbit game
item.description: arXiv:2610.18537v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the Hunters and Rabbit game, hunters shoot at a set of vertices at each round, while an invisible rabbit must move along an edge. We prove that deciding whether a given number of hunters can guarantee capture is PSPACE-complete, even on simple bipartite graphs. The reduction uses intersection nonemptiness for inverse finite automata: one common word must put all automata in accepting states simultaneously. A clique acting as a safe haven and two families of guards force every winning strategy to simulate common transitions. Existing transformations remove the restriction on the rabbit's initial positions and yield PSPACE-completeness for the directed game with one hunter, even on oriented graphs with positive minimum outdegree. Adjusting the guard sizes also proves PSPACE-completeness of the firefighting game, in which the rabbit may remain at its current vertex.
item.dc:creator: Walid Ben-Ameur, Alessandro Maddaloni

item.title: A Randomized Approximation Algorithm for Doubly Free-Boundary Macdonald Processes
item.description: arXiv:2610.18698v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We construct an approximate sampler for finite doubly free-boundary Macdonald rail-yard processes with Macdonald, boundary, and edge parameters in $(0,1)$. The construction allows arbitrary finite sequences of additions and removals of horizontal or vertical strips and all four boundary types. It reverses a finite commutation--reflection history from a partition sequence whose entries are equal, with the common partition weighted by both boundaries. We derive local reconstruction kernels from the skew Cauchy, Littlewood, and branching identities. Bulk and boundary updates combine integer increments with conditional shape sampling at a prescribed size; same-sign swaps use finite conditional resampling. For $K$ reflection periods and an initial partition-size cutoff $M$, the algorithm terminates almost surely and samples the resulting approximating law exactly. We prove total variation convergence to the target process as $K,M\to\infty$ and give explicit bounds for both truncation errors, decaying geometrically in the cutoffs for fixed input parameters. Under fixed parameter bounds, we also bound the expected operation count of direct enumeration in a unit-cost model. We further construct an exact rejection sampler for the initial partition law without a size cutoff or evaluation of its normalizing constant. Using this sampler removes the size-truncation error, leaving only the error from the finite reflection history.
item.dc:creator: Zhongyang Li

item.title: Robust Extensible Bin Packing and Revisiting a Convex Knapsack Problem
item.description: arXiv:2510.23765v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study a robust extensible bin packing problem, under a budget uncertainty model where item sizes lie in the intersection of a box with a one-norm ball. We design an algorithm based on the column-and-constraint generation framework, which alternates between solving a master robust bin-packing problem with a finite uncertainty set and solving a separation problem. We show that the separation is strongly NP-hard given solutions to the continuous relaxation of the master problem. Then, focusing on the separation problem for the integer master problem, we show that this problem becomes a special case of the continuous convex knapsack problem, which is known to be weakly NP-hard. Next, we prove that our special case remains NP-hard. We develop a pseudo-polynomial dynamic program (DP) and a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) for our special case whose running times match those of the binary knapsack problem. Finally, our computational study shows that the DP can be significantly more efficient in practice compared with solving the problem with specially ordered set (SOS) constraints using advanced mixed-integer programming (MIP) solvers. Our experiments also demonstrate the application of our separation problem method to solving the robust extensible bin packing problem, including separating based on approximate master solutions in intermediate iterations. We further enhance the algorithm by proposing custom symmetry breaking inequalities, valid when bins have identical costs per unit of excess capacity. Finally, a case-study, based on real elective surgery data, demonstrates the potential advantage of our model compared with the actual schedule and optimal nominal schedules.
item.dc:creator: Noam Goldberg, Michael Poss, Yariv Marmor

item.title: A Primal-Dual Approach to Randomized Online Bidding with Tail Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2610.05580v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Controlling tail risk in randomized algorithms has received increasing attention. Randomized online algorithms can achieve a lower expected competitive ratio than the competitive ratio of the best deterministic online algorithm. However, individual executions may still incur poor outcomes. Tail constraints address this risk by limiting the probability that the incurred ratio exceeds a prescribed threshold. We investigate how such constraints affect the structure and performance of randomized online bidding algorithms. By revisiting the classical primal-dual lower-bound framework for online bidding, we find that restricting the growth between consecutive bids can yield a stronger lower bound on the expected competitive ratio. We then show that tail constraints with zero exceedance probability impose an asymptotic upper bound on the ratios between consecutive bids. Incorporating this structural property into the primal-dual framework allows us to derive a stronger lower bound. Moreover, the dual analysis suggests a randomized geometric bidding algorithm whose performance matches this bound. The insight from our primal-dual analysis also guides the design of algorithms for general tail constraints allowing positive exceedance probabilities. Motivated by the geometric growth suggested by the dual solution, we study randomized periodic bidding algorithms. We show that, for any fixed geometric base, the uniform offset distribution is optimal in terms of both the expected competitive ratio and tail-constraint feasibility. We then characterize the exceedance probability of these algorithms and use this characterization to choose a geometric growth factor that satisfies the prescribed tail constraints, establishing parameter-dependent upper bounds on the optimal expected competitive ratio.
item.dc:creator: Royce Kraakman, Bob Krekelberg, Alison Hsiang-Hsuan Liu, Fu-Hong Liu

item.title: Boolean dimension and dim-boundedness: Planar cover graph with a zero
item.description: arXiv:2206.06942v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In 1989, Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il and Pudl\'ak posed the following challenging question: Do planar posets have bounded Boolean dimension? We show that every poset with a planar cover graph and a unique minimal element has Boolean dimension at most $10$. As a consequence, we are able to show that there is a reachability labeling scheme with labels consisting of $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ bits for planar digraphs with a single source. The best known scheme for general planar digraphs uses labels with $\mathcal{O}(\log^2 n)$ bits [Thorup JACM 2004], and it remains open to determine whether a scheme using labels with $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ bits exists. The Boolean dimension result is proved in tandem with a second result showing that the dimension of a poset with a planar cover graph and a unique minimal element is bounded by a linear function of its standard example number. However, one of the major challenges in dimension theory is to determine whether dimension is bounded in terms of standard example number for all posets with planar cover graphs.
item.dc:creator: Heather Smith Blake, Piotr Micek, William T. Trotter

item.title: Separable convex optimization over indegree polytopes
item.description: arXiv:2509.06182v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study separable discrete convex optimization over indegree vectors of orientations of an undirected graph, focusing on the effect of imposing acyclicity. Since the extreme points of the indegree polytope are precisely the indegree vectors of acyclic orientations, this amounts to comparing optimization over its integer points with optimization over its extreme points. Over all orientations, minimizing a vertex-separable discrete convex objective is strongly polynomial-time solvable by minimum-cost flow. Over acyclic orientations, for every fixed discrete convex function shared by all vertices, we obtain a dichotomy: if the function is linear on the positive integers, the problem is solvable in linear time; otherwise exact optimization is NP-hard on connected simple graphs, and APX-hard when the function is non-negative. We also give strongly polynomial-time constant-factor approximation algorithms for broad classes of convex and concave objectives. For the $p$-power sum of indegrees, this yields a $2^p$-approximation for every fixed integer $p\geq1$, while the problem is APX-complete for every fixed integer $p\geq2$; if $p$ is part of the input, no deterministic polynomial-time $2^{p^{1-\varepsilon}}$-approximation exists for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$ unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. We further give an exact $O(2^{|V|}|V|+\operatorname{poly}(|V|,|E|))$-time dynamic program for general separable objectives, with a matching lower bound in the exponent under the Exponential Time Hypothesis. Finally, decreasingly minimal and increasingly maximal acyclic orientations need not coincide and are both NP-hard, while minimizing the maximum weighted indegree over acyclic orientations remains strongly polynomial-time solvable.
item.dc:creator: N\'ora A. Borsik, P\'eter Madarasi

item.title: Emerging consecutive pattern avoidance
item.description: arXiv:2511.02442v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this note we study the asymptotic popularity, that is, the limit probability to find a given consecutive pattern at a random position in a random permutation in the eighteen classes of permutations avoiding at least two length 3 consecutive patterns. We show that for ten classes, this popularity can be readily deduced from the structure of the permutations. By combining analytical and bijective approaches, we study in detail two more involved cases. The problem remains open for five classes.
item.dc:creator: Nathana\"el Hassler, Sergey Kirgizov

item.title: Subexponential upper bound on the number of rich words
item.description: arXiv:2511.11069v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Let $R_q(n)$ denote the number of rich words of length $n$ over a fixed alphabet of size $q\geq2$. It is known that $R_q(n)^{1/n}\to1$. We establish a nonrecursive subexponential upper bound on the number of rich words, with its asymptotic growth quantified in terms of an iterated logarithm. For every $\lambda\in(1/2,1)$ and $\gamma>1$, there exists $c>0$ such that, for every positive function $\phi$ satisfying $\phi(n)\to\infty$ and $n/\phi(n)\to\infty$, the functions \[ f(n)=\left[c\ln^{*}\!\left(\frac{n}{\phi(n)}\ln q\right)\right]^{1/\gamma}, \qquad B(n)=q^{\frac{n}{\phi(n)}+\frac{n}{(2\lambda)^{f(n)-1}}} \] satisfy $R_q(n)\leq B(n)$ for all sufficiently large $n$ and $B(n)^{1/n}\to1$. Here $\ln^{*}$ is the iterated natural logarithm, with value zero on $(0,1]$. The proof iterates a counting inequality based on palindromic factorization and controls the resulting multiplicative constants using the iterated logarithm.
item.dc:creator: Josef Rukavicka

item.title: Flips and Merge-Width in Sparse Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2602.12926v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A flip of a graph is obtained by complementing the edge relation within a set of vertices. Flips are typically used to separate vertices in a graph, by increasing the distances between them. We show that in $K_{t,t}$-free graphs, every short sequence of flips can be simulated by a short sequence of vertex deletions that achieves a similar degree of separation: distances in the resulting graph are, up to a factor of three, at least as large as those obtained after the flips. This result provides a simple and uniform explanation of an emerging pattern in structural graph theory and finite model theory: the $K_{t,t}$-free fragment of a tameness notion for dense graphs often coincides with a tameness notion for sparse graphs. As immediate applications, we recover the following known equivalences. In the $K_{t,t}$-free setting, the dense notions (1) bounded shrub-depth, (2) bounded clique-width, (3) bounded flip-width, (4) monadic dependence, respectively, coincide with the sparse notions (1) bounded tree-depth, (2) bounded tree-width, (3) bounded expansion, and (4) no-where dense-ness. Furthermore, we reprove the result by Dreier and Toru\'nczyk (STOC 2025) stating that $K_{t,t}$-free classes of bounded merge-width have bounded expansion. Our proof provides explicit bounds and is direct, as it shows how to construct strong coloring orders (witnesses of bounded expansion) from merge sequences (witnesses of bounded merge-width). Along the way, we identify a new family of graph parameters, dubbed separation-width, that is sandwiched between the strong and weak coloring numbers, and is closely related to the merge-width parameters. We provide evidence that this family of graph parameters, apparently overlooked in the literature, may play a fundamental role in the study of sparse graphs.
item.dc:creator: Karolina Drabik, Ma\"el Dumas, Nikolas M\"ahlmann, Wojciech Przybyszewski, Szymon Toru\'nczyk

item.title: The Smallest String Attractors of Fibonacci, Period-Doubling, and Thue--Morse Words
item.description: arXiv:2602.16152v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A string attractor of a string $T[1..|T|]$ is a set of positions $\Gamma$ of $T$ such that any nonempty substring $w$ of $T$ has an occurrence that crosses a position in $\Gamma$, i.e., there is a position $i$ such that $w = T[i..i+|w|-1]$ and the intersection $[i,i+|w|-1]\cap \Gamma$ is nonempty. The size of the smallest string attractor of Fibonacci words and period-doubling words of length at least $2$ is known to be $2$. The size of the smallest string attractor of Thue--Morse words of length at least $25$ is known to be $4$. We completely characterize the set of all smallest string attractors of Fibonacci words, period-doubling words, and Thue--Morse words. For Fibonacci words, we show a recursive formula describing the $2^{n-4} + 2^{\lceil n/2 \rceil - 2}$ distinct position pairs that are the smallest string attractors of the $n$th Fibonacci word for $n \geq 7$. For period-doubling words, we show that the $n$th period-doubling word has exactly two smallest string attractors for every $n\geq 2$, and give them explicitly. For Thue--Morse words, we show a formula describing the 32 sets of four positions that are the smallest string attractors of the $n$th Thue--Morse word for $n\geq 6$. Our results show that strings with the same smallest attractor size can have a drastically different number of distinct smallest attractors.
item.dc:creator: Mutsunori Banbara, Hideo Bannai, Peaker Guo, Dominik K\"oppl, Takuya Mieno, Yoshio Okamoto

item.title: Non-Exclusive Notifications for Ride-Hailing at Lyft I: Single-Cycle Approximation Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2603.21533v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ride-hailing platforms increasingly rely on non-exclusive notifications--broadcasting a single request to multiple drivers simultaneously--to mitigate inefficiencies caused by uncertain driver acceptance. In this paper, the first in a two-part collaboration with Lyft, we formally model the Notification Set Selection Problem for a single decision cycle, where the platform determines the optimal subset of drivers to notify for each incoming ride request. We analyze this combinatorial optimization problem under two contention-resolution protocols: First Acceptance (FA), which prioritizes speed by assigning the ride to the first responder, and Best Acceptance (BA), which prioritizes match quality by selecting the highest-valued accepting driver. We show that welfare maximization under both mechanisms is NP-hard, ruling out a polynomial-time exact algorithm unless P=NP. Despite this hardness, we establish several positive algorithmic results. For FA, we develop a Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (PTAS) for the single-rider problem. For the general matching setting, we provide a (1-1/e)-approximation algorithm that applies to both FA and BA. Along the way, we show that the FA valuation function constitutes a novel discrete choice model with structural properties of independent interest. For BA, we further prove that the welfare objective is monotone and submodular and exploit additional structure to obtain an approximation guarantee that surpasses the classical (1-1/e) barrier. Finally, when acceptance probabilities are independent of the drivers, we show that the BA problem can be solved exactly in polynomial time through a linear programming formulation. We evaluate our algorithms on synthetic instances and on instances calibrated using real ride-sharing data from Lyft, demonstrating strong empirical performance.
item.dc:creator: Farbod Ekbatani, Rad Niazadeh, Shruti Penumatsa, Mehdi Golari, Romain Camilleri, Titouan Jehl, Chris Sholley, Matthew Leventi, Theresa Calderon, Angela Lam, Paul Havard Duclos, Tim Holland, James Koch, Shreya Reddy

item.title: Asymptotically Faster Algorithms for Recognizing $(k,\ell)$-Sparse Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2604.13025v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For fixed integers $k,\ell$ with $0\leq\ell<3k$, we study the problem of deciding whether a graph is $(k,\ell)$-sparse, a notion arising in combinatorial optimization and rigidity theory. Standard pebble-game algorithms take $O(n^2)$ time for $0\leq\ell<2k$ and $O(n^3)$ time for $2k\leq\ell<3k$, although faster algorithms were known for some parameter choices. We develop efficient recognition algorithms using bounded-indegree orientations, reductions to rooted arc-connectivity, augmenting paths, and centroid decomposition. For $0\leq\ell<2k$, they run in $O(n^{1+o(1)})$ time, yielding the first subquadratic bound valid throughout the entire range. Purely combinatorial implementations run in $O(n\sqrt n)$ time throughout this range. For graphs with $O(n)$ edges, we also improve the purely combinatorial running time for decomposing the edge set into a fixed number of forests, or certifying that no such decomposition exists, from $O(n\sqrt{n\log n})$ to $O(n\sqrt n)$. For simple graphs with $2k\leq\ell<3k$, the general recognition algorithm runs in $O(n^2)$ time when $\ell\leq2k+2$ and in $O(n^2\log n)$ time otherwise. When $\ell=2k$ and $k\leq3$, a specialized algorithm improves this to $O(n^{1+o(1)})$ and admits a purely combinatorial $O(n\sqrt n)$ implementation. Whenever the input graph is not $(k,\ell)$-sparse, our recognition algorithms return an explicit violating vertex set.
item.dc:creator: Bence De\'ak, P\'eter Madarasi

item.title: A Polynomial Kernel for Vertex Deletion to the Scattered Class of Proper Interval Graph and Trees
item.description: arXiv:2605.02399v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vertex deletion to the hereditary graph class has been well-studied in parameterized complexity. Vertex deletion in scattered graph classes has attracted attention in recent years. In this paper, we consider (PROPER-INTERVAL, TREE)-VERTEX DELETION, the input to which is an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ and an integer $k$. The goal is to pick a set $X \subseteq V(G)$ with at most $k$ vertices such that $G - X$ is a simple graph and every connected component of $G - X$ is a proper interval graph or a tree. When parameterized by the solution size $k$, (PROPER-INTERVAL, TREE)-VERTEX DELETION has been proved to be fixed-parameter tractable by Jacob et al. [JCSS-2023, FCT-2021]. Notably, (PROPER-INTERVAL, TREE)-VERTEX DELETION is a natural and substantial generalization of (CLIQUE, TREE)-VERTEX DELETION, which has been explored recently [JCSS-2026, ISAAC-2025, IPL-2025, ISAAC-2024]. The kernelization techniques for the latter exploit the finite forbidden induced subgraph characterization of cliques. In contrast, proper interval graphs and trees admit infinite forbidden induced subgraph characterizations, requiring new structural arguments. In this paper, we consider this problem from the perspective of polynomial kernelization and provide the first nontrivial polynomial kernel for (PROPER-INTERVAL, TREE)-VERTEX DELETION, with $O(k^{33})$ vertices.
item.dc:creator: Ashwin Jacob, Arpit Kumar, Diptapriyo Majumdar

item.title: Acyclic Dichromatic Number of Tournaments: these are the Champions
item.description: arXiv:2607.14694v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The acyclic dichromatic number of an oriented graph is the minimum size of a vertex-partition such that the digraphs induced by any single part are acyclic, and the oriented bipartite graphs between any two parts are acyclic too. We characterize the subtournaments that must appear in every tournament with sufficiently large acyclic dichromatic number, thereby confirming a conjecture of Bang-Jensen, Picasarri-Arrieta, and Yeo and prove that acyclic dichromatic number satisfies a local to global property.
item.dc:creator: Pierre Aboulker, Pierre Charbit, Samuel Coulomb, Kathryn Nurse, Lucas Picasarri-Arrieta

item.title: Linear Tur\'an Numbers of Uniform Hypertrees
item.description: arXiv:2607.16854v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A hypergraph is linear if every pair of vertices is contained in at most one hyperedge. We study linear Tur\'an numbers of acyclic $r$-uniform hypergraphs, extending earlier work of Gy\'arf\'as, Ruszink\'o, and S\'ark\"ozy from uniformity $3$ to general $r$, with emphasis on hypertrees with four hyperedges. For the linear path $P_4^r$, we prove $\operatorname{ex}^{\mathrm{lin}}_r(n,P_4^r)\le (r+1)n/r$, with equality precisely for disjoint unions of Steiner systems $S(2,r,r^2)$, whenever such systems exist. We also give counterexamples to a structural claim used in a previously proposed proof for $r=4$. The same bound and equality characterization hold for the broom $B_4^r$. For the crown $E_4^r$, writing $B=\{v:d(v)\le r\}$ and $C=\{v:r+1\le d(v)\le2r-1\}$, we prove $|E(H)|\le r|B|/(r-1)+(2r-1)|C|/r$, and hence $\operatorname{ex}^{\mathrm{lin}}_r(n,E_4^r)\le(2r-1)n/r$. We also give a lower-bound construction and formulate a sharper conjecture. Finally, for the linear star $S_k^r$, we prove $\operatorname{ex}^{\mathrm{lin}}_r(n,S_k^r)\le n(k-1)/r$, with equality precisely for $(k-1)$-regular linear $r$-uniform hypergraphs, whenever such hypergraphs exist. Under suitable divisibility and existence assumptions, we also construct $T_k^r$-free examples with $n(k-1)/r$ edges for every linear $r$-uniform hypertree $T_k^r$ with $k$ hyperedges.
item.dc:creator: Rajat Adak, Pragya Verma

item.title: Tight Approximation Thresholds for Geometric Stabbing
item.description: arXiv:2607.28062v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study geometric covering problems: stabbing axis-parallel squares and cubes by coordinate hyperplanes, stabbing horizontal segments by horizontal and vertical lines, and transversal of separated $d$-intervals. We prove matching NP-hardness bounds for their natural covering-LP thresholds. For every $\varepsilon>0$, square stabbing is NP-hard to approximate within $2-\varepsilon$, horizontal-segment stabbing within $e/(e-1)-\varepsilon$, and, for every fixed $d\ge2$, cube stabbing and separated $d$-interval transversal within $d-\varepsilon$. The results hold with finite candidate sets and when arbitrary admissible lines, hyperplanes, or track points are allowed. We construct harmonic integrality-gap families for squares and cubes and use the Kovaleva--Spieksma gap family for horizontal segments. In each family, every object meets a candidate of every orientation. We lift these gaps through the strict-CSP framework of Kumar, Manokaran, Tulsiani, and Vishnoi, using the Unique Games theorem to obtain NP-hardness. An ordered sampler preserves the LP marginals, coupled shifts make every local sample feasible, and a small perturbation through an absorbing label connects every local support. Cartesian cloning removes rational weights, after which disjoint blocks of candidate coordinates realize each output constraint by one square, cube, or horizontal segment. Applying the same transfer theorem to rectangle-hitting gaps of Pach and Tardos, we prove that stabbing axis-parallel boxes by supplied candidate lines in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is NP-hard to approximate within any fixed constant factor. Incidence-preserving algebraic maps yield the same hardness for hitting boxes in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and halfspaces in $\mathbb{R}^6$ by points from supplied finite candidate sets.
item.dc:creator: Khaled Elbassioni, Rishikesh Gajjala, Saurabh Ray

item.title: A Proof of Albertson's Conjecture
item.description: arXiv:2609.01682v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Albertson's conjecture states that every graph of chromatic number r has crossing number at least that of the complete graph K_r. We prove the conjecture for all r. The proof combines new clique-sensitive edge bounds for critical graphs, maximum-clique sampling, and a reserved immersion construction. For graphs of order close to r, we construct edge-disjoint routes while preserving a complete bipartite subgraph whose forced crossings compensate for those introduced when the immersion is smoothed into a drawing. For larger orders, we derive explicit edge bounds using independent-triple deletion and structural properties of critical graphs, then combine them with sampling inequalities that account for crossings within a maximum clique. The remaining numerical inequalities are certified using exact rational arithmetic, with a reproducible certificate and standalone Python verifier.
item.dc:creator: Ankan Sadhu

item.title: Simple symmetric Venn diagrams with 17, 19 and 23 curves
item.description: arXiv:2609.26546v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We exhibit simple, rotationally symmetric Venn diagrams with 17 curves, with 19 curves and with 23 curves: $n$ Jordan curves carried to one another by rotation through $2\pi/n$, with every one of the $2^n$ regions present and connected and, since the diagrams are simple, every crossing on exactly two curves. Symmetric Venn diagrams exist for every prime number of curves (Griggs, Killian and Savage, 2004), but those diagrams have many curves through a point; simple ones were known only up to 13 curves (Mamakani and Ruskey, 2014). Four 17-curve, twelve 19-curve and six 23-curve diagrams were found by a Metropolis walk on rotation-invariant quadrangulations of the sphere in which regions may temporarily be duplicated, started from the Griggs-Killian-Savage diagram with its multiple crossings resolved. At 23 curves the walk was held for two weeks by duplicated regions near the poles; the two lineages that finished were the first whose $E=92$ states had none. Every diagram is given by a machine-checkable certificate; one certificate each of the 17-, 19- and 23-curve sizes has been verified by a formal proof in Lean 4. All of the diagrams are non-monotone, which is why the crossing-sequence searches that found the 11- and 13-curve diagrams could not have found them.
item.dc:creator: Chris Dzoba

item.title: On the Binary Rank of Matrices with Constant Real Rank
item.description: arXiv:2609.30203v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the problem of determining upper bounds on the maximal binary rank, $b_d$, of a $0,1$ matrix with real rank $d$, for small constant $d$. We prove a general upper bound of $b_d \leq \left\lfloor \sqrt{d2^d + 2d}\right\rfloor -1$. We also develop a general dimension reduction technique of bounding $b_d$ using known upper bounds on $b_{d-1}$ and $b_{d-2}$, as well as prove interesting general structural results on extremal matrices with binary rank $b_d$. This allows us to get improved non-trivial upper bounds on $b_d$ for constant values of $d$, which imply tight bounds on $b_d$ for $3 \leq d \leq 5$. Our results also imply bounds on the equivalent problem of finding the minimum number of bicliques needed to partition the edges of a bipartite graph whose reduced adjacency matrix has real rank at most $d$.
item.dc:creator: Michal Parnas

item.title: W[1]-Hardness of Upper Clique Transversal
item.description: arXiv:2610.04917v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A clique transversal of a graph is a set of vertices intersecting every maximal clique. We prove that deciding whether a graph has an inclusion-wise minimal clique transversal of size at least $k$ is W[1]-hard when parameterized by $k$.
item.dc:creator: J. Pascal Gollin, Tesshu Hanaka, Ekkehard K\"ohler, Martin Milani\v{c}, Yushi Uno
